summary: Defines MIB objects to configure and monitor a Generalized MPLS Label Switching Router, the device that forwards traffic along label-switched paths.

eli5.summary: This is a dashboard for a GMPLS router. It lists the switches and gauges that show how the router forwards labeled traffic.

questions: what is the gmpls lsr mib
what is the gmpls label table
how to configure a bidirectional lsp with snmp
subtitle: The management tables for a GMPLS router's interfaces, segments and labels, including labels that do not fit in 32 bits.

tldr.problem: The MPLS LSR MIB could not describe everything a GMPLS router needs, such as bidirectional LSPs, per-interface signaling capabilities and labels that are longer than 32 bits or made of sub-fields.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4803 defines two MIB modules: GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB, which sparsely augments the interface and segment tables of RFC 3813, and GMPLS-LABEL-STD-MIB, with a gmplsLabelTable that stores generalized labels in one place.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure and monitor GMPLS routers over SNMP, including bidirectional LSPs and non-packet label types, while MPLS implementations can still reference the label table. It pairs with RFC 4802.

today: RFC 4803 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007, and no RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it. It is used together with RFC 4802.

sections.title: Introduction and Migration Strategy
sections.content:
RFC 4803 defines managed objects for modeling a Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR). MPLS LSRs are already managed with the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB module of RFC 3813. An LSR can migrate to the modules in this document to gain GMPLS support, or just to use extra objects that also help MPLS-TE.

The first module, GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB, extends the MPLS one through sparse augmentations of its tables. A migrating implementation only needs to add the new tables and objects, and the object gmplsInterfaceSignalingCaps lets it use them without supporting the GMPLS protocols. The second module, GMPLS-LABEL-STD-MIB, lets labels be configured and examined, and supports more label varieties. MPLS implementations can reference its labels through pointer objects such as mplsInSegmentLabelPtr without implementing GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB. The companion RFC 4802 does the same job for traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: It adds new pages to the router's existing control book, so a router can learn the fancier features one page at a time.

sections.title: Segments, Cross-Connects and Direction
sections.content:
An LSP is modeled as a connection made of one or more incoming segments (in-segments) and/or outgoing segments (out-segments) at an LSR. A cross-connect links them. Either set may be empty, for example when an LSP originates at this LSR. The RFC defines ingress/head-end, egress/tail-end, upstream, downstream, forward (ingress toward egress) and reverse (egress toward ingress).

For bidirectional LSPs, a single mplsXCIndex is shared by all segments of the whole LSP, which gives a simple reference from RFC 3812 and RFC 4802 and makes fate-sharing more obvious. To avoid connecting every in-segment to every out-segment, each segment carries a direction object: forward carries data from head to tail, reverse the other way. For manually configured LSPs an arbitrary choice of head and tail must be made, and for consistency it should be made the same across all participating LSRs.
sections.eli5: A road through a junction has lanes coming in and lanes going out. Each lane is marked either 'toward the destination' or 'back toward the start', so cars do not get mixed up.

sections.title: The GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB Tables
sections.content:
This module has three tables, each sparsely augmenting an RFC 3813 table so that a GMPLS entry shares the same index as its MPLS entry.

  • gmplsInterfaceTable enables GMPLS on MPLS-capable interfaces. gmplsInterfaceSignalingCaps is a bit set (unknown, rsvpGmpls, crldpGmpls, otherGmpls) with a default of rsvpGmpls; the RFC notes the use of CR-LDP is deprecated. Setting no bits means GMPLS signaling cannot be performed there and LSPs must be provisioned manually. gmplsInterfaceRsvpHelloPeriod is the period between RSVP Hello messages in milliseconds, default 3000, and 0 means send none.
  • gmplsInSegmentTable adds a direction and an optional pointer to extra technology-specific parameters (for example SONET resource usage).
  • gmplsOutSegmentTable adds the same two, plus gmplsOutSegmentTTLDecrement, the amount to decrement the TTL when per-hop decrementing is in use (0 means none).

Direction cannot be changed while the corresponding MPLS segment row is active.
sections.eli5: There is a page for each door of the box, and extra notes for every lane in and out: which way it goes and any special details.

sections.title: The GMPLS Label Table
sections.content:
The gmplsLabelTable in GMPLS-LABEL-STD-MIB manages generalized labels in one place. Generalized labels can have variable length and technology-specific bit meanings: labels for MPLS packet switching differ in length and content from labels for TDM timeslot switching. The table is used when the MplsLabel convention from RFC 3811 cannot hold the label (for example, it needs more than 32 bits), or when an operator wants to tell label types apart.

A row is identified by three indexes: gmplsLabelInterface (zero means the label applies system-wide), gmplsLabelIndex and gmplsLabelSubindex. The sub-index lets one label be a concatenation of sub-labels, useful in TDM; sub-labels are ordered by lowest sub-index first, and a label that is not concatenated should use zero.

gmplsLabelType says which value object is valid, for instance gmplsMplsLabel(1) (a packet label), gmplsPortWavelengthLabel(2) or gmplsFreeformLabel(3) (an octet string for labels that do not fit a standard encoding). Further objects cover SONET/SDH and waveband labels. Type and values cannot change while the row is active.
sections.eli5: Most lane tags are short numbers, but some are long or built from pieces. The notebook has room for any kind, and each entry says what kind it is.

sections.title: Configuring a Static Bidirectional LSP
sections.content:
For statically provisioned GMPLS LSPs the RFC lists the steps: configure an interface with the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB; enable GMPLS on it; configure in- and out-segments; add their GMPLS extensions; set up the cross-connect table; optionally create labels in the label table; and optionally set label stack actions and segment traffic parameters.

Its example makes a best-effort bidirectional LSP between interfaces with ifIndex 12 and 13. It creates one gmplsLabelTable row per interface, then in- and out-segments in RFC 3813 tables that point at those rows with label pointers (using createAndWait(5)), then marks each segment forward(1) or reverse(2). Two mplsXCTable rows join the segments, both with the same mplsXCLspId, and finally the segments are set to active(1).
sections.eli5: To build a two-way road you write down the tags, make the lanes, say which way each goes, connect them at the junction, and only then open it to traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The gmplsInterfaceTable, gmplsInSegmentTable, gmplsOutSegmentTable and gmplsLabelTable provision GMPLS interfaces, LSPs and their parameters. Unauthorized write access could disrupt traffic, especially for an LSP that is already established. The same tables also reveal the LSP topology and capabilities, so reading them may be sensitive.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and makes the operator responsible for giving access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can write in the notebook can reroute traffic, and anyone who can read it can see the map, so only trusted people should have access.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA rooted both modules under the mplsStdMIB subtree (1.3.6.1.2.1.10.166): GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB as number 15 and GMPLS-LABEL-STD-MIB as number 16. Future GMPLS-related standards-track MIB modules should be rooted under the same subtree, with new assignments only by Standards Action. The textual conventions used here are defined in RFC 4801.
sections.eli5: Each new page of the control book got an official page number from the keeper of numbers.
